n: In this lecture we introduce forensic thanatology. Thanatology, from the Greek thanatos, meaning death, is the branch of pathology that studies death and the processes associated with it. Forensic medicine studies mainly violent death, so the questions of thanatology occupy a central place in it. Remember: this knowledge is obligatory for every physician who may be called upon as a forensic medical expert or for expert actions.

Now the definitions of death. Death is the process of irreversible loss of the ability of the cerebral cortex to carry out higher nervous activity. By the traditional definition, it is the persistent, irreversible cessation of the vital functions of the organism and of the indices of homeostasis. The table gives three concepts. In brain death, higher nervous activity is irreversibly lost; in vegetative death, the vital functions irreversibly cease. Necrosis is partial death, meaning irreversible disorganisation of a part of a living organism.

Categories and kinds of death. By the socio-legal criterion, death is divided into two categories: non-violent, that is, from disease, and violent, that is, from external action. Violent death has three kinds: homicide, suicide and accident. It is important that establishing the category and kind falls within the competence not of the expert but of the investigating officers.

The three levels of the cause of death. The cause of death is the injury or disease that led to death, either by itself or through its complications. Establishing the cause is the main task of the forensic medical expert. First the immediate cause is determined, for example cerebral or pulmonary oedema, or shock. Then the intermediate cause is established, for example peritonitis or suppuration of a wound. Finally the underlying cause is found, that is, the underlying disease or injury, for example a skull fracture or an acute ulcer.

t: Case analysis: the chain of causes
n: Case analysis: the chain of causes. Consider an example: in a perforated gastric ulcer, peritonitis develops. Here peritonitis is the intermediate cause. The ulcer disease is the underlying cause, and the immediate cause is the morphological equivalent of the terminal disorder, for example shock. Now ask yourself: by which term will you name each link of this chain?

t: Structure of the forensic medical diagnosis
n: The structure of the forensic medical diagnosis. The forensic medical diagnosis is a set of judgements about injuries and diseases, and it is written in pathogenetic sequence. It consists of three parts: the underlying disease or underlying injury, its complications, and concomitant diseases. Remember: the diagnosis takes into account not only the cause but also the mechanism of death.

The mechanism of death, that is, thanatogenesis. This is the sequence of structural and functional disturbances, caused by a disease or injury, that leads to death. By thanatogenesis, death is divided into kinds such as death from brain, lung, heart, kidney, liver and adrenal gland failure. By frequency, the cardiovascular variant of thanatogenesis comes first.

The definition of death according to Simpson. Somatic death is understood to mean that the person will never again interact with the environment, and that unconsciousness is irreversible. The key word is “irreversible”. For deep sleep, anaesthesia, drugs or alcohol, and temporary coma also lose contact. In the United Kingdom there is no statutory definition of death; the courts have accepted the criteria of “brain death” for diagnosis.

Simpson: death and artificial ventilation. Previously, death of the brainstem led to cessation of breathing, then to myocardial hypoxia and cardiac arrest. Artificial ventilation interrupts this chain, that is, the heart does not stop during ventilation. There is also a spectrum of survival: some recover breathing and consciousness, while others need permanent ventilation.

t: Terminal states: preagonal state and terminal pause
n: Terminal states: the preagonal state and the terminal pause. In the preagonal state, consciousness and reflexes are almost absent, breathing is rapid and shallow, heart sounds are muffled, the pulse is thready, and blood pressure is low and continues to fall. In the terminal pause, consciousness, reflexes and breathing cease, the pulse cannot be detected, and blood pressure is close to zero. Compare the two stages and remember the difference.

Agony, clinical and biological death. The stages of dying follow one another: preagonal state, terminal pause, agony, clinical death, biological death. In agony, reflexes and even consciousness may briefly return, breathing is infrequent, deep and convulsive, the heartbeat quickens, and blood pressure rises slightly. In clinical death, consciousness, reflexes, breathing and cardiac activity are absent, but restoration of vital functions is still possible. Biological death is an irreversible disturbance of the structure and function of the brain.

Agony and agonal injuries. Agony is a set of pathophysiological processes reflecting disruption of the coordination of the homeostatic systems of the organism. Injuries received during agony are called agonal; the reaction to them is weaker than to injuries inflicted in other periods of life. Death that occurs in apparent good health without agony, or with very brief agony, is called sudden, in Russian “skoropostizhnaya” death.

Signs of rapidly occurring death. In rapid death the blood in the heart and vessels is fluid, and venous congestion and extensive cadaveric lividity are seen in the internal organs. There are fine punctate haemorrhages on the serous and mucous membranes, and autolysis develops in the pancreas. In prolonged agony, by contrast, the corpse contains many blood clots rich in fibrin. In the table you can see both variants side by side.

t: Signs for establishing the fact of death
n: Signs for establishing the fact of death. Consciousness and reflexes, that is, the corneal and pupillary reflexes, are absent; there is no electrical activity on the EEG and ECG; there is no pulse, heartbeat or breathing. In Beloglazov's sign, when the eyeball is pressed, the pupil becomes oval. This is a reliable criterion of death, and it appears within 10-15 minutes. But remember: only cadaveric changes are regarded as an indisputable sign.

Supravital reactions. These are reactions that persist for a certain time after death. Electromechanical reactions of the muscles disappear within 8-12 hours. Under the action of electric current, the whole facial musculature contracts at 2-3 hours, and only the orbicularis oris muscle at 3-5 hours. The pupillary reaction persists for up to 1.5 days, and the reaction of the sweat glands for 20 hours. These time limits are given in the table.

Early cadaveric changes: cooling. Cooling of the corpse is due to the fact that heat loss continues while the production of endogenous heat ceases. The temperature falls by an average of 1 °C per hour. Exposed parts of the body cool faster, and the temperature is measured in the axilla, the rectum and the liver tissue. The result of thermometry is usually assessed together with other findings, taking into account corrections such as clothing and body weight.

Cadaveric drying. Cadaveric drying is the result of continuing evaporation of water from the skin and mucous membranes and cessation of glandular secretion. Areas lacking a stratum corneum dry fastest: the sclera, the red border of the lips, and the surface of an abrasion. In open eyes, after 4-5 hours the cornea becomes cloudy, and Larcher's spots appear on the sclera.

Rigor mortis. Rigor is associated with redistribution of calcium and polymerisation of actomyosin, and begins at 2-6 hours. In the classical view it descends from the masticatory muscles downwards and reaches its maximum at 12-24 hours. Then, from the middle of the 2nd day, it begins to disappear, and has disappeared completely by day 3-7. Rigor of the heart is special: it begins at 2-3 hours and persists for 1.5-2 days.

Factors influencing rigor. Rigor is stronger in those who did physical labour, in major blood loss, and in convulsions in the pre-death period. It is weak in children and the elderly, and with some poisons, for example poisoning with the death cap. Rigor of the heart begins at 2-3 hours and persists for 1.5-2 days. If the heart has not undergone rigor, cardiac thanatogenesis is presumed.

Rigor and body position. If rigor is artificially broken in the first hours, it is restored, but more weakly. It is significant if the degree of rigor does not correspond to the time established from other signs. Another important sign: if rigor is absent in the upper limbs but present in the lower ones, the position of the corpse has been altered.

Cadaveric lividity develops in three stages. Hypostasis appears at 2-4 hours: it disappears on pressure, and shifts if the corpse is turned. Stasis occurs at 12-24 hours: it blanches on pressure, and if the corpse is turned over, two groups of patches form. Imbibition is observed at about the 2nd day: on pressure the colour does not change, and neither does the location. Remember the sequence of the stages.

The colour of lividity and hypostasis. The colour of the patches indicates a possible cause. In carbon monoxide poisoning, that is, CO, the patches are bright red. With cyanides the colour is cherry, and with methaemoglobin-forming agents a greyish-brown colour is seen. In those who died of cold and in bodies recovered from water the colour is pinkish-red. Cadaveric hypostasis is the post-mortem filling with blood of the dependent parts of the internal organs.

t: Case analysis: patches divided into two groups
n: Case analysis: patches divided into two groups. A corpse is found, and cadaveric lividity is present on both the back and the sides. In the stage of stasis, that is, at 12-24 hours, if the position is changed, part of the blood shifts, while the old patches remain. Question: what does this show, and what can be said about the time of death? Try to answer on your own.

Blood clotting and autolysis. After death the blood becomes fluid. In prolonged agony it may clot after 2 hours, whereas in rapid death it remains fluid because of fibrinolysis. Autolysis is the breakdown of tissues by their own proteolytic enzymes; the mucous membrane of the gastrointestinal tract and the pancreas are affected first. Histological assessment of autolysis is used in determining the time since death. After 6 hours, a disturbance of blood distribution appears.

t: Simpson: rigor and time of death
n: Simpson: rigor and time of death. Rigor is a temperature-dependent change that occurs in muscle cells because of lack of oxygen. In moderate conditions it is detectable in the face at 1-4 hours and in the limbs at 3-6 hours, with a maximum at about 18 hours. An important conclusion: rigor does not give the time of death precisely, so tables should be viewed with caution.

t: Simpson: temperature and the Henssge nomogram
n: Simpson: temperature and the Henssge nomogram. Three assumptions are made for temperature: the temperature at death was 37 °C, extrapolation is possible, and the ambient temperature is constant. On the Henssge nomogram the 95% confidence limit is at most 2.8 hours on either side of the most probable time. In addition, a change in ambient temperature of 5 °C can alter the time of death by at least 1 hour.

Late changes: putrefaction. Putrefaction is the decomposition of organic substances, especially proteins, by bacteria. The odour is noticeable as early as day 1. The green discoloration begins in the iliac region: at the end of day 1 in summer, and on days 2-3 in winter. Then putrefactive venous marbling and emphysema appear, and the body is bloated with gas. The sequence: putrefactive odour, green discoloration of the corpse, venous marbling, emphysema.

The corpse and insects. Flies, that is, Diptera, lay eggs. In 1-2 days larvae emerge and eat the tissues. In about a week the larvae pupate, and in 7-10 days the adult fly emerges. The length of the larva is measured, which is called larvometry; the length corresponds to the age of the larva. Then beetles arrive.

Preservation processes, that is, natural preservation. Adipocere forms in an environment with little oxygen and much moisture; full formation takes about 1 year. Mummification occurs in a dry, ventilated place; in an adult it does not occur earlier than 2-3 months. In a peat bog, humic acids soften the bone, while the microstructure is preserved for a long time.

t: Other methods of determining the time of death
n: Other methods of determining the time of death. When a more precise time is needed, indices such as pH and the concentration of potassium and calcium ions in the blood and vitreous humour are studied. In addition, hypoxanthine and creatinine in the vitreous humour, DNA degradation and enzyme activity are measured. Remember: the most accurate result is given by applying a combination of different methods.

t: The concept of the scene of the incident
n: The concept of the scene of the incident. The scene of the incident is the site or room where an event requiring legal assessment took place and which is subjected to investigative inspection. The discovery of a corpse is itself an incident, so the place where a corpse is found is always a scene of incident. Examination of the corpse at the scene is part of the scene inspection; the participants are the investigator and two witnesses.

The duties of the specialist physician. The specialist is a forensic medical expert or a physician with special knowledge; he must have no interest in the outcome of the case. His duties: to pronounce death or give first aid; to describe the position, clothing and appearance of the corpse. Also to describe the cadaveric phenomena and injuries, to assist in collecting biological evidence, and to give oral answers.

t: Static and dynamic stages of inspection
n: The static and dynamic stages of inspection. In the static stage the scene is studied without disturbance, described and photographed without touching objects. The corpse remains in place; its location and the arrangement of the body parts, that is, the posture, are recorded. In the dynamic stage, objects are picked up and carefully studied in rubber gloves. The inspection begins with the clothing.

t: Procedure for examining the corpse in the dynamic stage
n: The procedure for examining the corpse in the dynamic stage. The first step is the clothing: it is not removed at the scene, except when taken as evidence. The second step is the general description: sex, age, build, height. In the third step the cadaveric phenomena are described to a standard. In the fourth step, cooling, Larcher's spots, cadaveric lividity, rigor, muscle reactions and rectal temperature are recorded.

Description of injuries. The natural orifices, foreign bodies, external genitalia and bones are examined without rough movements. The site of the injury is indicated precisely; the type, that is, abrasion, bruise or wound, the shape, colour and dimensions are described. A wound is described by the clock face. Remember: a wound must not be probed, because a false track is created.

t: What cannot be decided at the scene
n: What cannot be decided at the scene. At the scene the time of death cannot be stated exactly, but an opinion can be given on whether the time indicated by a witness is possible. The cause of death is decided only after a complete forensic medical examination of the corpse. The group characteristics of the weapon are determined in the mortuary; at the scene, however, some weapons can be excluded.

t: Place where a newborn is found
n: The place where a newborn is found. The bodies of fetuses or newborns are found in various places; often they are wrapped in a newspaper, sheet or clothing. Items found with the body are described in detail; inscriptions, stamps and marks are sought, and the owner of the item is established. The items are preserved and handed over to the investigating authorities.

t: Simpson: cause of death and the certificate
n: Simpson: cause of death and the certificate. Establishing the cause of death is a judgement about causation; the cause must be “substantial and significant”, and without it the consequence would not have occurred. The certificate is drawn up in the WHO format. In Part I the conditions directly leading to death are entered, a, b, c; the disease at the bottom is the most important. In Part II other contributing conditions are indicated. It is not recommended to write the mode of death, for example coma or heart failure, on its own.

t: Simpson: manner of death and medico-legal investigation
n: Simpson: manner of death and medico-legal investigation. In some countries the manner of death, that is, homicide or suicide, is entered on the certificate, but in many Western countries this conclusion is left to a legal official. The English coroner has jurisdiction if the death is violent or unnatural, the cause is unknown, or the death occurred in custody. The coroner's court cannot express an opinion on criminal or civil liability.

t: Simpson: aims of the forensic autopsy
n: Simpson: aims of the forensic autopsy. An autopsy is carried out for two reasons: clinical interest and forensic purpose; the forensic autopsy is carried out on behalf of the state. Its aims: to identify the body, estimate the time of death, describe the number and nature of injuries, and detect diseases and poisons. Without an internal examination it is often impossible to state the cause and mechanism precisely; in at least a third of cases the causes given by physicians proved wrong at autopsy.
